posts.title: Raspberry — early growth, carefully slowed down
posts.content:
**What I did:** removed all dead, old canes; kept the plant bright and cool; avoided fertilizer; started short, daytime balcony exposure to improve light quality and harden the young growth, while bringing the pot back indoors overnight due to frost.

**Next steps:** continue controlled day–night acclimation until night temperatures stay above freezing. Once permanently outdoors and shoots reach 10–15 cm, begin light organic feeding. Later in spring, reduce the number of canes to a few strong shoots suited to the small container.
The focus right now is structure and resilience, not speed. Strong canes matter more than early growth.

posts.title: Raspberry — still alive, visibly rebooting; late-winter recovery
posts.content:
*The old canes look done, but the plant has started pushing fresh shoots from the base. That’s the real health indicator: it’s investing energy where it matters.*

**What I did:** removed fully dead, dry canes close to the soil line; kept watering conservative and consistent; no feeding yet; kept it bright but avoided “forcing” it with warmth.

**Next steps:** wait until the new shoots turn a deeper green and gain height. Once growth is stable (ideally after moving it outdoors for real light and airflow), start a mild, organic feed. Later in spring, reduce excess shoots so a few strong canes get all the energy. ~Rule of thumb right now: lightly moist soil, no swamp, no fertilizer.~

posts.title: Fig — woke up too early, premature budbreak
posts.content:
*The fig has already started leafing out, and a few early fruitlets are present. It’s not dying — it’s simply overly optimistic because indoor conditions feel like spring.*

**What I did:** did not prune; reduced watering; absolutely no fertilizer. The main goal is to slow it down, not encourage soft, weak growth.

**Next steps:** keep it as cool and bright as possible (cold window zone, away from heat sources). If outdoor placement becomes feasible without harsh frost, transition gradually and protect the pot from cold stress. Feeding only starts after stable spring conditions and steady leaf expansion.

~If some early fruitlets drop: normal. The priority is a strong plant, not February heroics.~

posts.title: Redcurrant (Jonkheer van Tets) — pruned and ready
posts.content:
*The plant is still in dormancy, buds are plump, and the framework is healthy. This is the ideal timing window for shaping in a container: fewer canes, better fruit quality.*

**What I did:** selected and kept **six main canes** for a clean, airy structure; removed weak/crowded growth; kept the short 5–10 cm side shoots intact (they’re productive on redcurrant).

**Next steps:** leave it alone now: bright, cool, and only minimal watering. Start a gentle, organic feed once leaf-out is clearly underway. After harvest, consider removing one of the oldest canes at the base to keep the plant young and productive.

~Container logic: remove wood rather than “topping” it. Short side shoots are assets, not clutter.~

posts.title: Meshtastic — Experimenting with Antenna Positioning
posts.content:
I plan experimenting with antenna positioning to improve both **transmit and receive performance** of my Meshtastic node. The conclusion is simple: *RF does not forgive sloppy geometry*.

**First rule:** polarization must match. Standard LoRa nodes operate with vertical polarization. The antenna must stand perfectly upright. 

~A 90° mismatch can introduce losses of up to 20 dB — not “a bit less range”, but “why is nothing arriving?”.~

At 868 MHz, physics is ruthless. Line of sight is king. Every additional meter of height often improves the link more effectively than increasing transmit power. 
*Windowsill > desk > floor. Balcony railing > inside the apartment. Mast > balcony.*

~The reason is the Fresnel zone: obstacles inside it attenuate signals subtly but dramatically. When testing, optimize height first — only then tweak antennas.~


**Keep clearance from metal:** 
- Maintain at least 1–2 cm distance to batteries, screws, ground planes, or enclosure hardware. 
- Do not mount a 18650 parallel and close to the antenna. 
- Do not press PCB ground planes against the radiator. 
- Do not route the antenna through metal. 
- Metal detunes the antenna, increases SWR, and reduces effective radiated power.

**Indoor environments are hostile:** 
- Reinforced concrete is a radio enemy. 
- Coated thermal windows behave like shields. 
- Radiators and refrigerators act as miniature Faraday cages. 
- If indoors, place the antenna near glass and avoid metal blinds.

~Outdoors is simple: free, high, vertical.~

**Cables introduce loss:**
At 868 MHz, expect roughly 0.3–0.6 dB attenuation per meter depending on cable quality. Thin, cheap coax can silently kill range. If possible, raise the node together with the antenna instead of extending the cable.

**Test realistically:** 
- Use fixed distances, 
- identical orientation, 
- and log RSSI and SNR. 
- Compare flat vs upright, 
- +1 m, +2 m, 
- window vs room. 
*You will be surprised how much difference even 30 cm can make.*


**Understanding RSSI and SNR is essential:**

**RSSI** (*Received Signal Strength Indicator*) measures **absolute received power in dBm** and includes signal, noise, and interference. **Typical LoRa values** range from −30 dBm (extremely strong) to −130 dBm (near sensitivity limit). *A high RSSI does not automatically mean a clean link.*

**SNR** (*Signal-to-Noise Ratio*) measures **signal clarity relative to noise** and can be positive or negative. 
- +10 dB is luxurious, 
- +5 dB stable, 
- 0 dB borderline, 
- −5 dB still functional. 
*LoRa can even decode below the noise floor — negative SNR is not magic, it is spread-spectrum processing gain.*

**Example comparisons:**
- RSSI −90 dBm / SNR +8 dB → strong and clean.
- RSSI −90 dBm / SNR −8 dB → strong but noisy.
- RSSI −120 dBm / SNR +7 dB → weak but clean, often more reliable than a noisy strong signal.

~RSSI tells you how loud it is. SNR tells you how clear it is.~

If RSSI is fine but SNR is poor, you likely face interference. If RSSI is weak but SNR is good, it is primarily a distance or geometry issue.


For 868 MHz LoRa (SF7–SF12), sensitivity typically ranges from −120 to −137 dBm depending on spreading factor. SNR thresholds can go down to roughly −20 dB at high spreading factors. A link with RSSI −125 dBm and SNR −10 dB can still work.

The biggest mistake is assuming: “*The antenna is good, so everything is fine.*”

~In reality, most range issues stem from incorrect polarization, insufficient height, building attenuation, or metal detuning — not firmware, transmit power, or channel configuration.~

posts.title: Meshtastic — Field Test with My Mobile Node
posts.content:
I took my new mobile Meshtastic node — 3D printed case, 18650 inside — for a walk and kept sending messages to my stationary node at home. *The experiment turned out to be more revealing than expected.*

**Not all messages were transmitted successfully.** 
- Some never arrived at all. 
- Others appeared to fail, triggered new send attempts, and were eventually delivered multiple times. 
- In one case, the same message was received four times. 
On the sender, however, only the very last transmission at 18:33 was visible. On the receiving node, all delivery attempts between 18:22 and 18:33 appeared individually.

The final message must have been a **direct transmission**, as it included the link parameters “SNR −12.25 dB” and “RSSI −133 dBm.” According to Google Maps, the straight-line distance was about 370 meters, with several buildings and dense trees in between. From my position, the home node was located behind the far-facing window — essentially on the shielded side of the building.

It was a small but very concrete reminder: LoRa works astonishingly well under harsh conditions, but reliability is not binary. Geometry, obstruction, retries, and marginal link budgets shape what actually arrives — and what only appears to have been sent.

posts.title: What this is about & Why I got into modding
posts.content:
Gothic modding is not about bigger swords, louder magic, or more spectacle. It is about **world logic**. A Gothic world works when its rules are consistent, its silences intentional, and its people behave as if they existed before the player arrived — and will continue after he leaves. Modding means learning how that illusion is built — and how to extend it without breaking the spell. 

I grew up with games that trusted the player to listen, observe, and think. Gothic was one of them. It never explained itself fully. It hinted. It implied. It expected attention. At some point, playing was no longer enough. I wanted to understand **why** a line of dialogue felt heavy, **why** a village felt hostile without anyone saying so, **why** a quest worked even when nothing “happened”. Modding was the natural next step: not to rewrite Gothic — but to speak its language fluently.

posts.title: What Gothic modding actually is
posts.content:
A Gothic mod is a **fan-made extension** built on the original engine. You do not replace the game — you converse with it. That conversation happens across several disciplines:

- logic (scripts)
- space (worlds)
- rhythm (NPC routines)
- restraint (knowing what not to add)

~Good mods feel like lost chapters. Bad mods feel like noise. ~



**Core disciplines**

**> Scripting (Daedalus)**
Daedalus is the nervous system of Gothic. Dialogue, quests, NPC behavior, attributes, routines — all of it lives here. It is not a forgiving language, but it is honest. If something breaks, it breaks for a reason. And once you understand that reason, you gain absolute control. Scripting teaches discipline: clear structure, explicit intent, no magic shortcuts.

**> World building (Spacer)**
The Spacer is where theory becomes geography. Every object — a torch, a pan, a windlass, a chair — must be placed with intent. Worlds are not “decorated”; they are **constructed**. Trigger zones, freepoints, paths, and interactions shape how the player moves without being told where to go. A good Spacer does not create scenery. He creates **habitable space**.

**> World building (Meshing)**
Custom worlds demand assets: meshes, textures, props, architecture. Today, Blender and modern toolchains make this accessible — but technical ability alone is not enough. Everything must fit Gothic’s visual grammar: rough, grounded, functional, slightly worn. If an object looks like it wants attention, it already failed.


**The roles behind a mod**
A functioning mod is rarely a solo act. Typical roles include:
- Scripter — logic, dialogue, quests, routines
- Spacer — world layout, object placement, flow
- 3D Artist — environments, items, architecture
- 2D Artist — textures, UI elements
- Concept & Audio — mood, coherence, restraint

~The key is not talent — it is coordination. Clear ownership beats creative chaos every time. ~


**Starting small (and why that matters)**
Everyone dreams of “*the next Gothic*”. That is the fastest way to fail. The first mod should be:

- short
- contained
- focused
- finishable

One village.
One storyline.
One or two hours of playtime.

~Anything more is ambition without structure — and Gothic punishes that mercilessly. ~


**Learning resources & community**
Gothic modding survives because knowledge is shared — slowly, meticulously, sometimes painfully. Wikis, forums, IRC channels, and long-forgotten guides still matter. Not because they are modern — but because they are **tested**. If you ask good questions, people will answer. If you ask lazy ones, the engine will teach you instead. 



**Philosophy**
Modding Gothic is not about self-expression. It is about **respect**. Respect for the engine’s limits. Respect for the player’s intelligence. Respect for silence, implication, and restraint. When it works, nobody says: "Nice mod." They say: "*This feels like Gothic*." And that is the highest *compliment* there is.

posts.title: Another day - another field experiment
posts.content:
~Why There Is No Chat History (And Why That’s Not a Bug)~

I recently ran a small field experiment:
15 short private messages, sent while walking in the direction of my home node. The mobile node showed “**RECEIVED**” — meaning the intended node acknowledged the message.
Back home, I connected to the stationary node.
Only the last three messages were there.
At first glance, that feels like a failure.
It isn’t.
It’s architecture.

**ACK ≠ Archive**

In Meshtastic there are two relevant acknowledgement states:
- **DELIVERED** → acknowledged somewhere in the mesh
- **RECEIVED** → acknowledged by the intended node

What it does **not** mean:
*“This message has been permanently stored in a chat history.”*

Meshtastic nodes are radios with RAM buffers — not servers.
They confirm packet reception. They do not maintain long-term message archives.
This distinction matters.


**What Actually Happens Internally**

Each message is:
- fragmented into LoRa frames
- assigned an ID
- possibly retried
- possibly forwarded over hops
- stored temporarily in RAM

Even a “10 character” message creates more internal traffic than one might assume.

Nodes:
- maintain routing tables
- keep duplicate-suppression caches
- handle acknowledgements
- rebroadcast when needed
RAM is finite. Old packets get evicted. FIFO. No sentimentality.

That explains why:
- Earlier messages (possibly with hops and retries) were overwritten
- The last three (direct link, stable SNR, zero hops) survived in the buffer

Nothing malfunctioned.
The system behaved exactly as designed.


**The Philosophical Reality of Mesh**

LoRa mesh is 
- Best effort delivery
- Opportunistic routing
- Minimal state retention

If you expect a messenger, you will be disappointed.
If you expect a resilient radio network, you will be impressed.


**The Real Question: How Do You Get Reliable Chat History?**
- Store & Forward Node
- MQTT Gateway (Turning Radio Into Data, this is where things get interesting)
- Direct Serial Logging (Simplest method: Connect the stationary node via USB to a PC or Raspberry Pi)

For now, I accept the system as it is, but the next step is clear. I want to add a memory to the mesh.
**And that’s a project for the near future.**

posts.title: When Ventilation Slots Start to “Melt”
posts.teaser: A simple kitchen sponge holder turned into a small lesson in physics and machine dynamics. What looked like clean, functional ventilation slots slowly transformed into something resembling stacked wet clay. Why do thin vertical structures suddenly lose their precision halfway up – and what does that reveal about temperature, cooling, and mechanical resonance in 3D printing?
posts.content_en:
While printing a kitchen sponge holder, I added vertical ventilation slots – thin columns designed to improve airflow and drying. Simple in theory. Not entirely in practice.

Around mid-height, the print quality visibly changed. The once smooth lines turned irregular. The material looked as if wet clay was being stacked upward instead of clean layer deposition.

~“Tall, thin features follow their own printing physics.”~

This behavior isn’t random and doesn’t mean the printer is defective. Slender vertical structures begin to oscillate slightly as they grow taller. Each new layer is deposited onto a structure that is no longer perfectly rigid. Combined with temperature, cooling, and speed, this leads to the characteristic “mud stacking” appearance.

Common causes:
- slightly too high extrusion temperature
- insufficient cooling
- not enough minimum layer time
- mechanical resonance
- printing thin features too fast

Possible improvements:
- reduce temperature by a few degrees
- slow down outer walls
- increase fan speed
- adjust minimum layer time
- print two objects simultaneously to allow better cooling

What started as a functional airflow detail became a small lesson in material behavior and machine dynamics.

And that is precisely why I enjoy 3D printing so much:
Every object teaches something new.

posts.title: Does my Meshtastic node really store only three direct messages? A field test
posts.content_en:
During a hiking test, I sent a series of messages from my mobile node to my stationary node – some as direct messages, others via a private channel. The goal was to test a specific assumption:

~The stationary node stores only the last three direct messages locally.~

On the mobile device, the full sequence is visible: “Neuer Test”, “Stoffbauer”, “Spiegel1/2”, “A Wildgans1/2”, “Sorger1/2”, “Pre-Hilmi1”, “2 hops Pre-Hilmi1”, “1 hop hilmwies”, “Runde ende”. The messages show proper ACK indicators – checkmarks and cloud icons – meaning they were acknowledged and delivered within the mesh.

However, on the stationary node the situation is different:

- In the direct chat (“Crno”), only
- “2 hops Pre-Hilmi1”
- “1 hop hilmwies”
- “Runde ende”
are visible.
- All earlier direct messages are missing.
- In the private channel chat, a much longer history is retained.

Signal metrics provide additional context. “2 hops Pre-Hilmi1” was received with SNR −13 dB and RSSI −133 dBm, which is near the sensitivity limit. “1 hop hilmwies” also showed negative SNR values around −6 to −7 dB and RSSI around −125 dBm. The final “Runde ende” message arrived with strong values (SNR above +10 dB, RSSI around −65 to −70 dBm).

The crucial point: Even messages received under good signal conditions are not retained beyond the last three entries. The ACK icons confirm delivery, yet the local storage is clearly limited.

This strongly suggests a RAM-based limitation for direct message history. Only the last three direct messages appear to be kept locally, while older ones are overwritten. Channel messages seem to follow a different retention behavior.

**Conclusion:**
Direct messages appear to be stored only temporarily. Anyone requiring reliable history should consider logging solutions, external storage, or systematic synchronization.

- „2 hops Pre-Hilmi1“

- „Runde ende“ 
sichtbar.
- Frühere Direktnachrichten fehlen vollständig.
- Im privaten Channel hingegen ist eine deutlich längere Historie vorhanden.

Die Funkwerte liefern zusätzlichen Kontext. Bei „2 hops Pre-Hilmi1“ wurden etwa SNR −13 dB und RSSI −133 dBm angezeigt – das ist bereits im Grenzbereich. Auch „1 hop hilmwies“ lag bei negativen SNR-Werten um −6 bis −7 dB und RSSI etwa −125 dBm. Die letzte Nachricht „Runde ende“ kam hingegen mit sehr guten Werten an (SNR über +10 dB, RSSI um −65 bis −70 dBm).

Entscheidend ist jedoch: Auch die mit guten Werten übertragenen älteren Direktnachrichten sind nicht mehr vorhanden. Die ACK-Symbole belegen, dass sie im Mesh angekommen sind. Dennoch werden sie nicht dauerhaft gespeichert.

Die Beobachtung spricht stark für eine RAM-basierte Begrenzung des Direktnachrichten-Speichers. Offenbar werden nur die letzten drei Einträge im lokalen Verlauf gehalten, ältere werden überschrieben. Channel-Nachrichten scheinen anders behandelt zu werden.

**Fazit:**
Direktnachrichten sind im aktuellen Setup offenbar nur temporär gespeichert. Wer eine verlässliche Chat-Historie benötigt, sollte über Logging-Strategien, externe Speicherung oder regelmäßige Synchronisation nachdenken.

posts.title: Every major endeavor starts quietly: with a list
posts.teaser: I’m beginning the Astronomy section of my website with a structured **catalog of significant stars** — the luminous anchor points of our night sky.
posts.content_en:
I am now beginning work on the Astronomy page — a section that will systematically explore stars, constellations, and their stories. The first step is deliberately foundational: building a structured collection of so-called “significant stars.”

**What are “significant stars”?**
These are particularly prominent stars that are historically, culturally, or astrophysically important — typically bright principal stars of a constellation (often designated with the Bayer label α), navigation stars, members of well-known asterisms such as the Summer or Winter Triangle, or stars with extraordinary physical properties. They are the fixed points in the sky that provide orientation — both literally and metaphorically.

**My list will be built systematically:**
Name, alternative designations, linguistic origin (often Arabic or Latin), mythological context, astronomical classification, and constellation affiliation. The foundation is a structured compilation similar to the existing document, which I am now consolidating digitally, expanding, and gradually transforming into a searchable, well-referenced overview.

**Why this focus?**
Because an astonishing amount converges in a single star:
– cultural history (Arabic star names, Greek mythology, medieval star charts)
– navigation and calendrical systems
– astrophysics (distance, spectral class, luminosity, multiple star systems)
– and not least, the pure aesthetic presence of the night sky.

Whether Arcturus as the brightest star of the northern sky, Sirius as the radiant benchmark, or Deneb as the distant giant of the Summer Triangle — each of these stars is both an anchor point in the cosmic structure and a chapter of human history.

In the next phase, the list will move beyond description toward contextualization: Which geometric relationships exist? Which stars form triangles, quadrilaterals, hexagons? Which lie close to the ecliptic and are occulted by the Moon or planets? Which are astrophysically remarkable — red giants, multiple systems, nearby stellar neighbors?

The Astronomy page will therefore not become a loose collection, but a structured star map in textual form — growing, precise, and driven by the ambition not merely to observe the sky, but to understand it.
posts.content_de:
**Große Vorhaben beginnen oft unspektakulär: mit einer Liste.**

Ich starte nun mit dem Aufbau meiner Astronomy-Seite – ein Bereich, der sich systematisch mit Sternen, Sternbildern und ihren Geschichten beschäftigen wird. Der erste Schritt ist dabei bewusst grundlegend gewählt: eine strukturierte Sammlung sogenannter „significant stars“.

**Was sind „significant stars“?**
Gemeint sind besonders auffällige, historisch, kulturell oder astrophysikalisch bedeutsame Sterne – meist helle Hauptsterne eines Sternbildes (oft mit der Bayer-Bezeichnung α versehen), Navigationssterne, Bestandteile markanter Asterismen wie Sommer- oder Winterdreieck, oder Sterne mit außergewöhnlichen physikalischen Eigenschaften. Es sind jene Fixpunkte am Himmel, die Orientierung stiften – im wörtlichen wie im übertragenen Sinn.

**Meine Liste wird systematisch aufgebaut:**
Name, alternative Bezeichnungen, sprachliche Herkunft (oft arabisch oder lateinisch), mythologischer Kontext, astronomische Einordnung sowie die Zugehörigkeit zum jeweiligen Sternbild. Die Grundlage bildet eine strukturierte Sammlung ähnlich dem bestehenden Dokument, die ich nun digital konsolidiere, erweitere und perspektivisch in eine durchsuchbare, sauber referenzierte Übersicht überführen möchte.

**Warum dieser Fokus?**
Weil sich an einzelnen Sternen erstaunlich viel bündeln lässt:
– Kulturgeschichte (arabische Himmelsnamen, griechische Mythologie, mittelalterliche Sternkarten)
– Navigation und Kalenderwesen
– Astrophysik (Entfernung, Spektralklasse, Leuchtkraft, Mehrfachsysteme)
– und nicht zuletzt die reine Ästhetik des Nachthimmels.

Ob Arktur als hellster Stern des Nordhimmels, Sirius als strahlender Maßstab, oder Deneb als ferner Gigant des Sommerdreiecks – jeder dieser Sterne ist ein Ankerpunkt im kosmischen Gefüge und zugleich ein Kapitel Menschheitsgeschichte.

In einem nächsten Schritt soll die Liste nicht nur beschreibend sein, sondern kontextualisiert werden: Welche geometrischen Beziehungen bestehen? Welche Sterne bilden Dreiecke, Vierecke, Sechsecke? Welche sind ekliptiknah und werden von Mond oder Planeten bedeckt? Welche sind physikalisch besonders interessant – Rote Riesen, Mehrfachsysteme, Nachbarsterne?

Die Astronomy-Seite wird damit kein loses Sammelsurium, sondern eine strukturierte Sternenkarte in Textform – wachsend, präzise, und mit dem Anspruch, den Himmel nicht nur zu betrachten, sondern zu verstehen.

posts.title: Handheld astronomy on the Plabutsch — smartphone astrophotography attempt
posts.teaser: Photographing the waxing Moon through binoculars turned out to be far more chaotic (and rewarding) than expected.
posts.content_en:
I recently took my smartphone up to the Plabutsch and tried something slightly ambitious: photographing the waxing Moon through my Swarovski binoculars.

- No tracking mount.
- No tripod adapter.
- No proper phone holder.

Just patience, steady hands, and a good amount of stubbornness.

Aligning a phone camera with binocular optics sounds simple — until you try it. The slightest movement shifts the entire frame. The Moon disappears. The focus jumps. The exposure blows out. And then you start again.

*It was, quite frankly, a bit of a pain.*

But in between frustration and micro-adjustments, something interesting happened: a few surprisingly detailed shots emerged. Mare structures became visible. The terminator showed texture. Even a wide-field frame captured a passing aircraft crossing the sky near the Moon — an accidental but beautiful contrast between celestial permanence and human motion.

- Technically imperfect? Yes.
- Rewarding? Absolutely.

This little experiment also sparked an idea: instead of wrestling optics with bare hands, I might design and 3D-print a dedicated smartphone holder for my binoculars. A simple adapter could transform this chaotic setup into something reproducible — and much sharper.

~Sometimes progress starts with annoyance.~

**More attempts will follow.**
posts.content_de:
**Zunehmender Mond am Plabutsch — Smartphone durch das Fernglas**

Ich war am Plabutsch unterwegs und habe versucht, den zunehmenden Mond mit meiner Handykamera durch mein Swarovski-Fernglas zu fotografieren.

- Ohne Adapter.
- Ohne fixe Halterung.
- Ohne Stativ.

Nur mit Geduld, ruhiger Hand und einer gewissen Portion Trotz.

Was in der Theorie simpel klingt, ist in der Praxis erstaunlich mühsam. Die Kamera exakt über die Austrittspupille zu positionieren, ohne dass der Mond wieder aus dem Bild springt, ist eine Geduldsprobe. Minimalste Bewegungen ruinieren den Fokus. Die Belichtung kippt sofort ins Überstrahlte. Und dann beginnt das Ausrichten von vorne.

*Kurz gesagt: Es war ein ziemlicher Pain in the Ass.*

Und trotzdem sind einige wirklich interessante Aufnahmen entstanden. Mare-Strukturen sind klar erkennbar, der Terminator zeigt schöne Kontraste, und in einer Weitwinkelaufnahme kreuzt sogar ein Flugzeug mit Kondensstreifen das Bild — ein spannender Kontrast zwischen Technik und Himmelskörper.

Technisch nicht perfekt, aber atmosphärisch stark.

Das Ganze hat mich auf eine Idee gebracht: Warum nicht eine maßgeschneiderte Handy-Halterung für das Fernglas mit dem 3D-Drucker entwerfen? Ein sauberer Adapter würde das Setup stabilisieren und die Wiederholbarkeit massiv verbessern.

~Manchmal beginnt ein neues Projekt genau dort, wo etwas nervt.~

**Fortsetzung folgt.**

posts.title: Redcurrant — leaf damage from winter acclimation stress (not night frost)
posts.teaser: Winter sun can be a liar: bright light plus cold, dry air stressed my currant during balcony acclimation — crispy edges, curled leaves, and a clear reminder to harden off slower.
posts.content_en:
Since December my currant (Ribisel) has been living indoors. From late January on, I started a careful “hardening off” routine: daytime trips to the balcony/loggia (south-facing, wind-sheltered, partly shaded), always brought back inside before night.

**What I’m seeing:** curled leaves and dry, crispy tips/edges.

**Most likely cause:** *acclimation stress* — cold air + low winter humidity + bright sun. Even without night exposure, winter days can combine strong radiation with chilly, dry air. The leaves transpire, the roots stay comparatively cold and slow, and the plant can’t keep up → desiccation-like damage (looks like “burn”, but it’s basically dehydration under cold conditions).

**What I did:**
- Kept soil evenly moist (not wet), avoided swings between bone-dry and soaked
- Continued sheltered outdoor exposure, but reduced duration when conditions were harsh (cold + bright)
- Checked for obvious pests on the leaf undersides (none found so far)

**Next steps:**
- Slow the hardening-off down: shorter outdoor sessions, preferably on milder days; avoid sharp midday sun when it’s cold
- Keep it wind-protected (wind = instant moisture theft)
- Don’t fertilize yet (new soft growth would just suffer again)
- Remove only fully dead leaf parts; leave partly green tissue until new growth starts
- If symptoms keep spreading despite gentler exposure: inspect closely for aphids/spider mites and consider a rinse/shower + soap solution
posts.content_de:
Seit Dezember steht meine Ribisel in der Wohnung. Ab Ende Jänner habe ich sie tagsüber regelmäßig auf die Loggia/Balkon gestellt (Südausrichtung, windgeschützt, teilweise beschattet) – **nachts war sie nie draußen**.

**Symptome:** eingerollte Blätter, braune/vertrocknete, „crispy“ Blattspitzen und -ränder.

**Wahrscheinlichste Ursache:** *Abhärtungsstress im Winter* – kalte Luft + trockene Winterluft + helles Sonnenlicht. Auch ohne Nachtfrost können Wintertage tückisch sein: Die Blätter verlieren Wasser (Transpiration), während der Wurzelballen in der Kälte träge bleibt. Ergebnis: Trockenstress-Schäden, die wie „Verbrennung“ wirken, aber im Kern eine Art Austrocknung unter Kältebedingungen sind.

**Was ich gemacht habe:**
- Erde gleichmäßig feucht gehalten (nicht nass), keine extremen Gieß-„Wellen“
- Draußen nur geschützt und bei Bedarf kürzer, wenn kalt + hell zusammenkamen
- Blattunterseiten auf Schädlinge geprüft (bisher nichts Auffälliges)

**Nächste Schritte:**
- Abhärtung entschleunigen: kürzere Zeitfenster, eher an milderen Tagen; grelles Mittagslicht bei kalter Luft meiden
- Weiter strikt windgeschützt halten
- Noch nicht düngen
- Nur vollständig abgestorbenes Material entfernen; halbgrüne Blätter erst später ausputzen
- Falls es trotz Schonprogramm weiter fortschreitet: gezielt auf Blattläuse/Spinnmilben kontrollieren, ggf. abduschen + milde Seifenlösung

posts.title: Entering the Airspace: My First Steps into Drone Flying
posts.teaser: After weeks of comparisons, rule-checking, second-guessing and spreadsheet-level overthinking, I finally stepped into the world of drone flying — cautiously, curiously, and with a strong preference for staying under 250 grams.
posts.content_en:
I’ve been circling around the idea of getting a drone for months.

Not impulsively — quite the opposite. In typical fashion, I dissected the topic from every possible angle: weight classes, flight restrictions in urban areas, battery life, image quality, upgrade paths, long-term motivation. The romantic image of cinematic sunset shots over the sea met the sobering reality of controlled airspace maps and city limits.

Living in Graz adds friction. You don’t just take off anywhere. Height limits matter. Open spaces matter. Distance from restricted zones matters. And suddenly, 30 meters stop sounding low — they start sounding reasonable. Roughly the height of a ten-storey residential building. Enough for perspective. Not enough for recklessness.

Very quickly, one constraint crystallized: under 250 g. That weight class isn’t magic, but it simplifies life. Lighter drone, fewer limitations, more spontaneity. The decision framework shifted from "What’s the most powerful drone?" to "What will I realistically fly often?"

I compared the usual suspects: compact entry-level models versus more capable ‘Pro’ variants. The temptation to overbuy was real. Better sensor. More dynamic range. Stronger wind resistance. But also: higher cost, more hesitation, more fear of crashing something expensive.

FPV fascinated me — the immersion, the speed, the almost visceral feeling of flight. But I had to be honest with myself: my primary goal is storytelling. Sailing footage. Landscape impressions. Calm, deliberate movement. Not racing through forests at 80 km/h.

So I chose an entry point that feels proportionate. Affordable enough to actually use. Capable enough to produce meaningful footage. Limited enough to force composition over spectacle.

What surprised me most wasn’t the technology. It was the mindset shift. Drone flying isn’t just buying hardware — it’s negotiating space. Reading wind. Respecting invisible borders. Accepting that sometimes you drive an hour for twenty minutes of flight time.

And because this isn’t a one-off experiment but a new strand of exploration, I’ve created a dedicated **Drone** subcategory under *Outdoor*. From now on, every flight log, lesson learned, comparison, and experiment will live there — structured, documented, and evolving.

It’s not just about flying. It’s about building a body of experience.

Is this the beginning of a long-term obsession? I don’t know yet.

But it’s a new axis in my creative toolkit. Between sailing, 3D printing, electronics, and Meshtastic experiments, this feels like the missing aerial perspective — literally.

For now, I’m learning restraint.
Low altitude. Slow movements.
Clean lines.
And the quiet satisfaction of seeing familiar places from a slightly different angle.
posts.content_de:
Seit Monaten kreise ich um die Idee, mir eine Drohne zuzulegen.

Nicht impulsiv – ganz im Gegenteil. In gewohnter Manier habe ich das Thema aus allen denkbaren Blickwinkeln seziert: Gewichtsklassen, Flugbeschränkungen im urbanen Raum, Akkulaufzeit, Bildqualität, Upgrade-Pfade, langfristige Motivation. Das romantische Bild von cineastischen Sonnenuntergängen über dem Meer traf auf die nüchterne Realität von Luftraumkarten und Stadtgrenzen.

In Graz zu leben erzeugt Reibung. Man startet nicht einfach irgendwo. Höhenlimits zählen. Freiflächen zählen. Abstände zu sensiblen Zonen zählen. Und plötzlich klingen 30 Meter nicht mehr niedrig – sie klingen vernünftig. Ungefähr die Höhe eines zehnstöckigen Wohnhauses. Genug für Perspektive. Nicht genug für Übermut.

Sehr schnell kristallisierte sich eine Leitplanke heraus: unter 250 g. Diese Gewichtsklasse ist kein Zaubertrick, aber sie vereinfacht das Leben. Leichtere Drohne, weniger Einschränkungen, mehr Spontaneität. Der Entscheidungsrahmen verschob sich von „Was ist die leistungsstärkste Drohne?“ zu „Was werde ich realistisch oft fliegen?“

Ich habe die üblichen Kandidaten verglichen: kompakte Einsteigermodelle versus leistungsfähigere ‚Pro‘-Varianten. Die Versuchung, zu viel zu kaufen, war real. Besserer Sensor. Mehr Dynamikumfang. Stabiler bei Wind. Aber eben auch: höhere Kosten, mehr Hemmung, mehr Angst, etwas Teures zu beschädigen.

FPV hat mich fasziniert – die Immersion, die Geschwindigkeit, dieses fast körperliche Fluggefühl. Aber ich musste ehrlich mit mir sein: Mein primäres Ziel ist Erzählen. Segelaufnahmen. Landschaftseindrücke. Ruhige, bewusste Bewegungen. Nicht mit 80 km/h durch Wälder zu jagen.

Also habe ich einen Einstieg gewählt, der sich verhältnismäßig anfühlt. Günstig genug, um sie tatsächlich zu nutzen. Leistungsfähig genug, um sinnvolle Aufnahmen zu produzieren. Begrenzend genug, um Komposition über Spektakel zu stellen.

Was mich am meisten überrascht hat, war nicht die Technik. Es war die mentale Verschiebung. Drohne fliegen heißt nicht nur Hardware kaufen – es heißt Raum verhandeln. Wind lesen. Unsichtbare Grenzen respektieren. Akzeptieren, dass man manchmal eine Stunde fährt, um zwanzig Minuten zu fliegen.

Und weil das kein einmaliges Experiment, sondern ein neuer Erkundungsstrang ist, habe ich unter *Outdoor* eine eigene Subkategorie **Drone** eingerichtet. Dort werden künftig alle Flugprotokolle, Erkenntnisse, Vergleiche und Experimente gesammelt – strukturiert, dokumentiert und im Wachsen begriffen.

Es geht nicht nur ums Fliegen. Es geht darum, Erfahrung aufzubauen.

Ob das der Beginn einer langfristigen Obsession ist? Ich weiß es noch nicht.

Aber es ist eine neue Achse in meinem kreativen Werkzeugkasten. Zwischen Segeln, 3D-Druck, Elektronik und Meshtastic-Experimenten fühlt sich das wie die fehlende Luftperspektive an – im wörtlichen Sinn.

Im Moment lerne ich Zurückhaltung.
Geringe Höhe. Langsame Bewegungen.
Klare Linien.
Und die stille Zufriedenheit, vertraute Orte aus einem leicht veränderten Blickwinkel zu sehen.

posts.title: Weather Display — Part I: A Small Station That Remembers
posts.teaser: A compact OLED weather station is simple. A compact OLED weather station with a **real-time clock, 24-hour ring buffer, and versioned EEPROM persistence** is where it stops being a demo and starts being engineering.
posts.content_en:
This project started with a simple but consequential question: what is the value of a weather display that forgets everything after a power loss?

So I built a compact Arduino-based weather station that displays **temperature, humidity, pressure, date and time** on a 128×32 SSD1306 OLED — and stores a full **24-hour history persistently in EEPROM**.

At first glance, the hardware is conventional:

- Arduino (Uno/Nano/Pro Mini compatible)
- BME280 (I²C 0x76)
- SSD1306 OLED (I²C 0x3C)
- DS3231 RTC with battery backup
- Two navigation buttons (D3 / D9)

All devices share the same I²C bus (SDA A4, SCL A5 on Uno/Nano), separated only by address.

The design goal, however, was continuity.

Timekeeping is handled by a DS3231 real-time clock instead of relying on millis(). This ensures stable time across resets and allows precise hourly aggregation.

Sensor values are internally stored as **int16_t scaled by ×10** (e.g. 23.5°C → 235). This keeps memory usage predictable, avoids floating-point overhead in the main logic, and eliminates dynamic String allocation.

The system maintains three 24-slot arrays:

- temp_messungen[24]
- humid_messungen[24]
- baro_messungen[24]

Each slot represents one hour. When the hour changes, the averaged value of the previous hour is written into the corresponding index. The arrays behave as a ring buffer.

To survive resets, the complete dataset is written to EEPROM as a structured image consisting of:

- Magic number (0xBEE5)
- Layout version
- Fletcher-16 checksum
- Payload (24h arrays + state variables)

On boot, the system validates the image before restoring data. If the checksum or version fails, the arrays remain initialized.

This first part outlines the concept and architectural decisions. In the next entries, I will go deeper into:

- the sampling and averaging strategy
- the EEPROM layout and integrity checking
- EU daylight saving time handling
- graph rendering on a 128×32 display under tight constraints

Small hardware. Strict structure. Persistent data.
posts.content_de:
Dieses Projekt begann mit einer einfachen, aber entscheidenden Frage: Welchen Wert hat eine Wetteranzeige, die nach einem Stromausfall alles vergisst?

Also entstand eine kompakte Arduino-basierte Wetterstation, die **Temperatur, Luftfeuchtigkeit, Luftdruck, Datum und Uhrzeit** auf einem 128×32 SSD1306 OLED darstellt — und einen vollständigen **24-Stunden-Verlauf dauerhaft im EEPROM speichert**.

Die Hardware ist zunächst klassisch:

- Arduino (Uno/Nano/Pro Mini kompatibel)
- BME280 (I²C 0x76)
- SSD1306 OLED (I²C 0x3C)
- DS3231 RTC mit Batterie-Backup
- Zwei Navigationstaster (D3 / D9)

Alle Komponenten teilen sich denselben I²C-Bus (SDA A4, SCL A5 bei Uno/Nano), getrennt ausschließlich durch ihre Adresse.

Der eigentliche Fokus lag jedoch auf Kontinuität.

Die Zeitbasis übernimmt eine DS3231-Echtzeituhr statt millis(). Dadurch bleibt die Zeit auch nach Resets stabil und stündliche Aggregation wird exakt möglich.

Messwerte werden intern als **int16_t im ×10-Format** gespeichert (z. B. 23,5 °C → 235). Das reduziert Speicherbedarf, vermeidet unnötige Floating-Point-Operationen im Kernsystem und verhindert Heap-Probleme durch dynamische Strings.

Das System verwaltet drei 24-Slot-Arrays:

- temp_messungen[24]
- humid_messungen[24]
- baro_messungen[24]

Jeder Slot repräsentiert eine Stunde. Beim Stundenwechsel wird der gemittelte Wert der vorherigen Stunde in den entsprechenden Index geschrieben. Die Arrays arbeiten als Ringpuffer.

Damit die Daten Resets überstehen, wird der komplette Zustand als strukturiertes EEPROM-Image gespeichert, bestehend aus:

- Magic Number (0xBEE5)
- Layout-Version
- Fletcher-16-Prüfsumme
- Payload (24h-Arrays + Statusvariablen)

Beim Start prüft das System Integrität und Version. Ist das Image ungültig, bleiben die Arrays initialisiert.

Teil 1 beschreibt Konzept und Architektur. In den nächsten Beiträgen folgen:

- Sampling- und Mittelwertstrategie
- EEPROM-Layout und Integritätsprüfung
- EU-Sommer-/Winterzeit-Logik
- Graphendarstellung auf 128×32 Pixeln unter Ressourcenbeschränkung

Kleine Hardware. Strikte Struktur. Persistente Daten.

posts.title: Weather Display — Part II: Clean Architecture on an 8-Bit Microcontroller
posts.teaser: An Arduino sketch can quickly become a monolithic loop. This project separates orchestration, hardware logic, persistence, and rendering — deliberately structured, even on an 8-bit microcontroller.
posts.content_en:
Most Arduino projects begin — and end — inside a single .ino file.

That works for blinking LEDs. It does not scale for a system that samples sensors, aggregates values, renders graphs, handles daylight saving time, debounces buttons, and persists structured data to EEPROM.

So this project is deliberately split into three layers:

- **main.ino** → orchestration
- **bme_sensor.cpp** → system logic
- **bme_sensor.h** → configuration + interface contract

---

## 1. main.ino — the conductor

`main.ino` contains almost no real logic. It initializes peripherals and coordinates execution.

Key responsibilities:

- Initialize Wire (I²C)
- Call `setupPins()` and `setupPeripherie()`
- Prime averaging buffers
- Restore EEPROM state
- Run the main execution loop

The `loop()` function does not compute values directly. Instead, it delegates:

- `CheckZeitumstellung()` → DST handling
- `doMeasurements()` → sensor sampling
- `saveHourlyMeasurements()` → hourly persistence
- `handleButtonInput()` → navigation
- Rendering functions → display output

This keeps the loop readable and predictable.

---

## 2. bme_sensor.cpp — the system brain

All operational logic lives here:

- Sampling and rolling averages
- Hourly accumulation
- Ring buffer updates
- Graph scaling and pixel mapping
- EEPROM layout and checksum validation
- DST logic

Instead of scattering logic across the sketch, everything with state lives in one translation unit.

Global variables are declared in the header but defined once in the .cpp file. This avoids duplicate definitions while keeping visibility explicit.

Example:

```cpp
extern int16_t T, H, P;
```

The header defines the contract. The implementation defines the memory.

---

## 3. bme_sensor.h — configuration and structure

The header is not just prototypes. It centralizes configuration:

- Display dimensions
- Button pins
- Timing constants
- Buffer lengths
- Feature flags (DEBUG, FIX_TIME_ONCE, INDICATOR_LED)

This makes the system tunable without rewriting logic.

Constants like:

```cpp

constexpr uint8_t numberOfMeassurements = 5;
```

ensure compile-time determinism and eliminate magic numbers.

---

## 4. Integer-first design

Sensor data is stored internally as `int16_t` scaled by ×10.

Why?

- Predictable RAM usage
- Faster arithmetic on AVR
- No float accumulation errors for stored values
- Minimal EEPROM footprint

Float conversion happens only at display or scaling boundaries.

---

## 5. Timer discipline

Instead of delay(), the system uses millis()-based timing:

- `meassure_timer`
- `button_timer`
- `timer` (auto-rotation)

This keeps the system non-blocking and ensures button input, measurement, and rendering coexist cleanly.

---

## 6. Separation of concerns — even here

- Rendering functions do not read sensors.
- Sensor functions do not draw pixels.
- EEPROM logic does not depend on display state.

Each module has a single responsibility.

On an 8-bit MCU with limited RAM, structure is not luxury — it is survival.

Part 3 will dive into the sampling strategy and how minute-based measurements become stable hourly averages.

posts.title: Hilltop Link Test — Citywide Coverage from Stefanienwarte
posts.teaser: From the Stefanienwarte overlook, I tested real-world Meshtastic performance: multi-hop routes, marginal SNR at distance, and surprisingly strong line-of-sight returns across the city.
posts.content_en:
I hiked up to the Stefanienwarte — not primarily for the view (though the winter panorama over the city was impressive), but for something more technical: altitude.

A hilltop is not just scenic. It is RF leverage.

From this elevated position overlooking the entire urban basin, I ran a series of transmission tests between my mobile unit and my stationary node at home.

**Observed link characteristics:**
- Direct city-facing transmissions showed strong returns: RSSI around -65 to -70 dBm with SNR > 10 dB.
- More obstructed directions dropped significantly: RSSI between -125 and -135 dBm, SNR down to -14 dB.
- Several packets successfully routed via 1–2 hops when line-of-sight degraded.
- Repeated "ping" messages confirmed route stability.

The data tells a clear story.
Height matters. Geometry matters. Urban attenuation is real — but so is mesh resilience.

One particularly interesting pattern: when positioned toward the open valley side, the link quality improved drastically. When facing denser terrain and structural obstructions, performance dropped but did not collapse — the mesh compensated via intermediate nodes.

This was not a laboratory test.
Cold air, wet snow underfoot, fluctuating conditions.

And yet: stable bidirectional communication.

The takeaway is simple and satisfying:
A well-placed stationary node combined with a modest elevation gain creates city-scale coverage without infrastructure.

Meshtastic in its purest form — decentralized, opportunistic, topology-driven.

The skyline was the backdrop.
The mesh was the real view.

Topografie schlägt Sendeleistung.

posts.title: Weather Display — Part III: From Raw Sensor Noise to Stable Hourly Averages
posts.teaser: Reading a sensor every 200 ms is easy. Turning that into stable, meaningful hourly data — without blocking the system or overflowing memory — requires structure.
posts.content_en:
A raw BME280 reading is not yet information. It is a moment.

This project transforms short-interval measurements into stable hourly values using a layered aggregation strategy designed for constrained hardware.

---

## 1. Fast sampling — but controlled

The sensor is read every 200 ms:

```cpp
constexpr uint8_t WAIT_TIME_MEASSURE = 200;
```

Instead of using delay(), the system relies on millis()-based timing. This keeps the loop non-blocking and allows measurement, rendering and button handling to run concurrently.

Each reading is written into small rolling buffers:

- tempsforMittelwert[5]
- humidsforMittelwert[5]
- pressuresforMittelwert[5]

The index cycles from 0 to 4 and wraps around.

---

## 2. Short-term smoothing

Every ~3 seconds (WAIT_TIME_MITTELWERT = 3000 ms), the system calculates a local mean:

```cpp
mittelwerte_berechnen(T, H, P, ...);
```

This produces stable values for:

- T (temperature ×10)
- H (humidity ×10)
- P (pressure ×10)

The averaging uses int32_t accumulation to prevent overflow before division.

This removes short-term sensor jitter while preserving responsiveness.

---

## 3. Minute-level accumulation

Instead of immediately writing values to the 24-hour arrays, the system aggregates per minute.

Whenever the RTC minute changes:

```cpp
if (old_minute != right_now.minute()) {
    hourlyMittelwertTemp  += T;
    hourlyMittelwertHygro += H;
    hourlyMittelwertBaro  += P;
    hourlyMittelwertCounter++;
}
```

Each minute contributes exactly one averaged value to the hourly accumulator.

This ensures consistent temporal weighting — independent of loop timing jitter.

---

## 4. Hourly finalization

When the hour changes, the accumulated sums are divided by the counter and written into the corresponding slot:

```cpp
temp_messungen[old_hour] = T_var / hourlyMittelwertCounter;
```

After that:

- Counters are reset
- old_hour is updated
- EEPROM persistence is triggered

Each array has 24 slots. The index corresponds directly to the hour of the day (0–23).

The system behaves as a ring buffer across days.

---

## 5. Why this layered model?

Because it balances three constraints:

1. Noise reduction
2. Temporal accuracy
3. Memory safety

Immediate storage would amplify jitter.
Pure second-level averaging would drift.
Direct float accumulation would waste RAM.

The layered design keeps arithmetic predictable and storage compact.

---

## 6. Deterministic memory footprint

All stored values are int16_t ×10.

Hourly accumulators use int32_t.

No dynamic memory allocation is involved.

On an AVR-class MCU, predictability is more important than elegance.

---

The result is not just a display — it is a structured data pipeline running on an 8-bit controller.

Part 4 will dive into how those 24 hours survive power loss using a versioned EEPROM image and a Fletcher-16 checksum.

---

Der Sensor wird alle 200 ms ausgelesen:


```cpp
mittelwerte_berechnen(T, H, P, ...);
```

Das liefert stabile Werte für:

## 3. Minutenweise Akkumulation

Die 24h-Arrays werden nicht direkt beschrieben. Stattdessen wird minutenweise aggregiert.

Sobald sich die RTC-Minute ändert:


## 4. Abschluss zur vollen Stunde

Beim Stundenwechsel werden die aufsummierten Werte durch den Zähler geteilt und in den entsprechenden Slot geschrieben:

```cpp
temp_messungen[old_hour] = T_var / hourlyMittelwertCounter;
```

3. Speichersicherheit

Reine Sekundenmittel würden driftanfällig.
Float-Akkumulation würde RAM verschwenden.

Das Schichtenmodell hält Arithmetik vorhersagbar und Speicher kompakt.

---

## 6. Deterministischer Speicherbedarf

Alle gespeicherten Werte sind int16_t ×10.

Stundenakkumulatoren nutzen int32_t.

Es gibt keine dynamische Speicherallokation.

Auf einem AVR-Mikrocontroller ist Vorhersagbarkeit wichtiger als formale Eleganz.

Das Ergebnis ist mehr als eine Anzeige – es ist eine strukturierte Datenpipeline auf einem 8-Bit-System.

posts.title: Weather Display — Part IV: EEPROM Architecture and Data Integrity
posts.teaser: Storing values in EEPROM is easy. Storing them in a way that survives corruption, version changes, and invalid layouts — that is where structure matters.
posts.content_en:
A 24-hour weather history is only useful if it survives resets.

Writing raw arrays into EEPROM is trivial. Writing them in a structured, versioned and verifiable format is deliberate engineering.

This project uses a complete EEPROM image consisting of:

- Header
- Payload
- Checksum

---

## 1. Structured layout

The EEPROM image is defined as:

```cpp
struct EepromHeader {
  uint16_t magic;
  uint8_t  version;
  uint8_t  reserved;
  uint16_t checksum;
};

struct EepromPayload {
  int16_t temp[24];
  int16_t humid[24];
  int16_t baro[24];
  int16_t old_hour_saved;
  int16_t old_day_saved;
};

struct EepromImage {
  EepromHeader  hdr;
  EepromPayload data;
};
```

The header protects the payload.
The payload contains exactly what must survive resets.

No hidden offsets. No implicit assumptions.

---

## 2. Magic number

```cpp
constexpr uint16_t EEPROM_MAGIC = 0xBEE5;
```

The magic value distinguishes valid data from random memory content.

If the value does not match, the system refuses to load the image.

This protects against:

- First boot (empty EEPROM)
- Flashing new firmware
- Memory corruption

---

## 3. Versioning

```cpp
constexpr uint8_t EEPROM_VERSION = 3;
```

If the internal layout changes in future revisions, the version number prevents old images from being interpreted incorrectly.

Backward compatibility is explicit.
Not accidental.

---

## 4. Fletcher-16 checksum

Before writing, a Fletcher-16 checksum is calculated over the payload bytes:

```cpp
uint16_t fletcher16(const uint8_t* data, size_t len)
```

On boot:

- The image is read.
- Magic and version are validated.
- The checksum is recalculated.
- Only if all checks pass is the payload applied.

This prevents partially written or corrupted data from being trusted.

Lightweight, deterministic, sufficient for this scale.

---

## 5. Size verification

Before loading or saving, the system checks:

```cpp
if (EEPROM.length() < sizeof(EepromImage))
```

If the device EEPROM is too small, persistence is disabled safely.

No undefined behavior.

---

## 6. Write discipline

EEPROM writes are not performed in every loop.

`saveMeasurementsToEEPROM()` is triggered only when a new hourly value is finalized.

This:

- Reduces wear
- Keeps write frequency predictable
- Avoids unnecessary flash cycles

On AVR, EEPROM.put() writes only changed bytes.

---

## 7. Deterministic memory footprint

All stored values are int16_t ×10.

The entire image size is fixed at compile time.

No dynamic allocation.
No pointer arithmetic in application logic.

The EEPROM image behaves like a small, versioned database record.

---

This is not just data persistence.
It is controlled state restoration.

Part 5 will examine EU daylight saving time handling and why relying on "month checks" is insufficient.
posts.content_de:

Arrays roh ins EEPROM zu schreiben ist trivial. Sie strukturiert, versioniert und überprüfbar zu speichern, ist bewusstes Engineering.

Das EEPROM-Image ist definiert als:

## 6. Schreibdisziplin

- vermeidet unnötige Flash-Zyklen

Keine Pointer-Arithmetik in der Anwendungslogik.

posts.title: Weather Display — Part V: Daylight Saving Time Done Properly
posts.teaser: Daylight saving time is not a "month check". It is a precise rule: last Sunday, exact hour, exactly once. Even small systems deserve correct time handling.
posts.content_en:
Timekeeping is easy — until it isn’t.

If a system stores hourly data, a one-hour error propagates into corrupted history. Daylight saving time (DST) cannot be handled with "if month >= 3" shortcuts. It must follow the exact rule.

This project implements EU DST transitions explicitly and defensively.

---

## 1. The rule

European DST transitions:

- Last Sunday in March, 02:00 → 03:00
- Last Sunday in October, 03:00 → 02:00

Not earlier. Not later. Not twice.

---

## 2. Detecting the last Sunday

Instead of hardcoding dates, the system checks:

```cpp
bool isLastSundayOfMarch(const DateTime& dt) {
  return dt.month() == 3 &&
         dt.dayOfTheWeek() == 0 &&
         (dt.day() + 7) > 31;
}
```

Logic:

- Month must match
- Day must be Sunday (0)
- Adding 7 days would exceed the month length

This reliably identifies the last Sunday without lookup tables.

---

## 3. Exact trigger condition

Adjustment only happens when all conditions match:

- Correct month
- Correct last Sunday
- Exact hour (02:00 or 03:00)
- Exact minute and second

Example:

```cpp
if (!sommerzeit &&
    isLastSundayOfMarch(dt) &&
    dt.hour() == 2 && dt.minute() == 0 && dt.second() == 0)
```

No drifting adjustments. No approximations.

---

## 4. Protection against double adjustment

A critical detail: without protection, the condition would remain true for an entire second — potentially causing repeated adjustments.

The system prevents this using a day marker:

```cpp
static uint16_t lastAdjustYday = 65535;
```

The day-of-year is derived from:

```cpp
uint16_t yday = DateTime(dt.year(), dt.month(), dt.day()).unixtime() / 86400;
```

If `yday == lastAdjustYday`, the system refuses another adjustment.

This guarantees exactly one transition per calendar day.

---

## 5. Why not rely on the RTC alone?

The DS3231 keeps time accurately — but it does not automatically apply DST rules.

Handling DST in firmware ensures:

- Correct hourly aggregation
- Consistent ring buffer indexing
- No duplicated or skipped hourly slots

Incorrect DST logic would misalign stored data for an entire day.

---

## 6. Defensive design

Each adjustment ends with a `return;` to prevent cascading logic in the same loop cycle.

The system explicitly tracks `sommerzeit` state instead of recalculating assumptions.

This makes the time logic:

- deterministic
- traceable
- easy to verify

---

Time errors compound quietly.

A single incorrect hour corrupts aggregation, persistence, and graphs.

On small systems, precision is not overengineering — it is responsibility.

Part 6 will explore how 24 hours of data are rendered meaningfully on a 128×32 OLED display.
posts.content_de:
Zeitmessung ist einfach – bis sie es nicht mehr ist.

Wenn ein System stündliche Daten speichert, propagiert ein Fehler von einer Stunde direkt in den Verlauf. Sommerzeit lässt sich nicht mit "wenn Monat >= 3" behandeln. Sie folgt einer präzisen Regel.

Dieses Projekt implementiert die EU-Sommerzeitumstellung explizit und defensiv.

---

## 1. Die Regel

EU-Umstellungen:

- Letzter Sonntag im März, 02:00 → 03:00
- Letzter Sonntag im Oktober, 03:00 → 02:00

Nicht früher. Nicht später. Nicht mehrfach.

---

## 2. Erkennung des letzten Sonntags

Statt feste Daten zu verwenden, prüft das System:

```cpp
bool isLastSundayOfMarch(const DateTime& dt) {
  return dt.month() == 3 &&
         dt.dayOfTheWeek() == 0 &&
         (dt.day() + 7) > 31;
}
```

Logik:

- Monat stimmt
- Wochentag ist Sonntag (0)
- In sieben Tagen wäre der Monat vorbei

So wird der letzte Sonntag zuverlässig erkannt – ohne Tabellen.

---

## 3. Exakte Auslösebedingung

Die Anpassung erfolgt nur, wenn alle Bedingungen erfüllt sind:

- Richtiger Monat
- Letzter Sonntag
- Exakte Stunde (02:00 oder 03:00)
- Exakte Minute und Sekunde

Beispiel:

```cpp
if (!sommerzeit &&
    isLastSundayOfMarch(dt) &&
    dt.hour() == 2 && dt.minute() == 0 && dt.second() == 0)
```

Keine Annäherungen. Keine Drift.

---

## 4. Schutz vor Doppelanpassung

Ohne Schutz würde die Bedingung eine ganze Sekunde lang wahr bleiben – mit mehrfacher Anpassung.

Das System nutzt daher einen Tagesmarker:

```cpp
static uint16_t lastAdjustYday = 65535;
```

Der Tag-im-Jahr wird berechnet über:

```cpp
uint16_t yday = DateTime(dt.year(), dt.month(), dt.day()).unixtime() / 86400;
```

Stimmt `yday` mit `lastAdjustYday` überein, erfolgt keine erneute Umstellung.

So wird exakt eine Anpassung pro Kalendertag garantiert.

---

## 5. Warum nicht allein auf die RTC verlassen?

Die DS3231 hält Zeit sehr genau – aber sie kennt keine Sommerzeitregeln.

Die Firmware-Logik stellt sicher:

- korrekte Stundenaggregation
- konsistente Ringpuffer-Indizes
- keine doppelt oder fehlend gespeicherten Stunden

Fehlerhafte DST-Logik würde einen kompletten Tagesverlauf verschieben.

---

## 6. Defensive Struktur

Nach jeder Anpassung folgt ein `return;`, um weitere Logik im selben Loop-Zyklus zu verhindern.

Der Zustand `sommerzeit` wird explizit verwaltet.

Das macht die Zeitlogik:

- deterministisch
- nachvollziehbar
- überprüfbar

Zeitfehler wirken leise – aber nachhaltig.

Auf kleinen Systemen ist Präzision kein Luxus, sondern Pflicht.

Teil 6 widmet sich der Darstellung: 24 Stunden Daten sinnvoll auf 128×32 Pixel abbilden.

posts.title: Raspberry after winter indoors — surprisingly healthy
posts.teaser: A raspberry that spent winter indoors is now showing vigorous new basal growth. The foliage is somewhat pale and slightly soft, but overall the plant looks healthy and ready for its full transition outdoors.
posts.content_en:
This raspberry spent the winter indoors in the living room, with occasional trips outside for gradual hardening. A slightly odd setup perhaps — but not an entirely unsuccessful one.

A few days into brighter spring conditions, the plant is now showing a fairly clear response. Several fresh shoots are emerging directly from the base, and that alone is a good sign: the root system is active, the plant has reserves, and it is trying to move forward rather than merely survive.

The leaves look structurally sound. I see no obvious pest damage, no fungal spotting, and no major deformities. What is noticeable, however, is the very light green color. The foliage is paler than ideal and the growth somewhat soft. That is not especially mysterious: winter indoors usually means less light, and less light tends to produce stretched, gentler growth with lower chlorophyll density.

So this is not a sick raspberry. It is a raspberry that grew under civilized but suboptimal conditions.

The good news is that this is usually reversible. Once it remains outside consistently, receives stronger light, and settles into a proper spring rhythm, the newer growth should become sturdier and darker.

For now, the next steps are simple:

- keep it outdoors consistently, provided temperatures stay reasonable
- give it a light dose of fertilizer or compost
- observe how many new canes develop and thin them later if needed

One other thing is already becoming apparent: raspberries are not shy about occupying a pot. If growth continues like this, a larger container will likely be necessary later in the season.

At the moment, though, the verdict is reassuring. The plant looks healthy, the pale foliage is explainable, and the transition from indoor wintering to outdoor growth seems to be working.

~Sometimes plants endure our improvisations with more dignity than we do.~
posts.content_de:
Diese Himbeere hat den Winter im Wohnzimmer verbracht – mit gelegentlichen Ausflügen nach draußen zur schrittweisen Abhärtung. Ein etwas eigenwilliges Setup vielleicht, aber keineswegs ein völlig verfehltes.

Einige Tage unter helleren Frühlingsbedingungen später zeigt die Pflanze nun eine recht klare Reaktion. Mehrere frische Triebe kommen direkt aus der Basis, und das ist bereits ein gutes Zeichen: Das Wurzelsystem ist aktiv, die Pflanze verfügt über Reserven und versucht nicht bloß zu überleben, sondern weiterzuwachsen.

Die Blätter wirken strukturell gesund. Es sind keine offensichtlichen Schädlingsspuren zu sehen, keine Pilzflecken und keine gravierenden Verformungen. Auffällig ist allerdings das sehr helle Blattgrün. Das Laub ist blasser als ideal, der Wuchs insgesamt etwas weich. Das ist kein großes Rätsel: Winter im Innenraum bedeutet meist Lichtmangel, und Lichtmangel führt oft zu gestrecktem, zarterem Wachstum mit geringerer Chlorophylldichte.

Es handelt sich hier also nicht um eine kranke Himbeere. Es ist eine Himbeere, die unter höflichen, aber botanisch nicht ganz idealen Bedingungen überwintert hat.

Die gute Nachricht: Das lässt sich meist korrigieren. Sobald sie dauerhaft draußen steht, mehr Licht bekommt und in einen normalen Frühlingsrhythmus findet, sollte der neue Austrieb kräftiger und dunkler werden.

Die nächsten Schritte sind daher recht schlicht:

- nun möglichst konsequent draußen lassen, sofern die Temperaturen vernünftig bleiben
- moderat düngen oder etwas Kompost geben
- beobachten, wie viele neue Ruten sich entwickeln, und später bei Bedarf auslichten

Noch etwas wird bereits sichtbar: Himbeeren sind im Topf nicht gerade bescheiden. Wenn das Wachstum so weitergeht, wird im Lauf der Saison vermutlich ein größeres Gefäß nötig werden.

Im Moment lautet das Urteil jedenfalls: beruhigend. Die Pflanze wirkt gesund, das helle Laub ist gut erklärbar, und der Übergang von der Innenraum-Überwinterung zum Wachstum im Freien scheint zu funktionieren.

~Manche Pflanzen ertragen unsere Improvisationen würdevoller, als wir selbst es tun.~

posts.title: Weather Display — Part VI: Rendering 24 Hours on 128×32 Pixels
posts.teaser:
~A 24-hour history is useless if the display turns it into static. On a 128×32 OLED, every pixel has to justify its existence.~

This stage of the project focused on one brutally practical question: how to render **temperature, humidity and pressure history** on a screen that barely has enough space for a sentence. The answer was not decoration, but restraint: fixed spacing, careful scaling, rotated buffer access, and just enough labels to keep the graph intelligible.
posts.content_en:
Displaying raw numbers is easy. Displaying *change over time* is harder — especially on a tiny monochrome OLED.

The goal here was to show **24 hours of history** in a way that remains readable at a glance. That forced a few design decisions that are simple in code, but decisive on screen.

~Tiny displays are unforgiving. They expose every lazy design choice immediately.~

The first constraint was geometry. The history buffer contains 24 values, so the rendering uses a simple horizontal spacing of three pixels per slot.

- one value per hour slot
- x-position based on a constant step
- enough spacing to preserve visual separation
- still compact enough to fit inside 128 pixels

That means the graph stays narrow, predictable, and legible instead of collapsing into a compressed mess.

The second decision concerns data order. Internally, the values live in a 24-slot ring-style history. For display, I do not reshuffle or copy the array. Instead, the renderer changes the starting index and walks through the data cyclically.

- storage stays simple
- rendering stays chronological
- no extra memory juggling
- the display window rotates naturally with the current hour

That is one of those small implementation details that quietly saves a lot of nonsense.

Humidity and pressure use **adaptive scaling**. The renderer scans the stored values, ignores empty entries, determines the real minimum and maximum, then derives a middle and a usable range. From that it computes a vertical drawing step.

- empty slots are skipped
- min and max come from actual data
- the scale adapts to recent conditions
- a minimum drawing step prevents absurd over-zooming

Without that lower bound, a barely changing pressure curve would balloon into theatrical nonsense. With it, the graph remains calm and honest.

The vertical mapping is centered rather than bottom-aligned. Instead of pinning everything to a base axis, values are drawn relative to a middle line.

- center-based mapping improves trend readability
- small variations remain visible
- the graph feels balanced instead of crushed to one edge

This matters especially when conditions are stable and the changes are subtle.

Temperature is treated differently on purpose. It uses a **fixed scale** instead of adaptive zoom.

- visual consistency across time
- easier comparison between different days
- no misleading exaggeration from narrow ranges

A temperature graph should not panic just because the room changed by half a degree.

The final piece is context. A graph without reference values is decoration pretending to be information. So the renderer prints three guide values on the right side.

- maximum
- middle value, or average in temperature mode
- minimum

The values are formatted in fixed-point style, which keeps the output precise without dragging float formatting everywhere through the code.

At startup, some history entries are still empty. Those are simply ignored.

- no garbage lines
- no fake zeroes
- the graph grows naturally over the first 24 hours

That makes the display robust from the first boot onward instead of only becoming useful a day later.

In the end, this part of the project became less about graphics and more about discipline. On a display this small, there is no room for visual vanity. Every line has to carry meaning.

~Part VII will close the build with lessons learned, tradeoffs, and the list of things that clearly deserve a V2.~
posts.content_de:
Zahlen anzeigen ist leicht. *Veränderung über Zeit* sichtbar zu machen, ist deutlich schwieriger — besonders auf einem winzigen, monochromen OLED.

Das Ziel war, **24 Stunden Verlauf** so darzustellen, dass man ihn auf einen Blick erfassen kann. Dafür waren einige Gestaltungsentscheidungen nötig, die im Code schlicht wirken, auf dem Display aber den ganzen Unterschied machen.

~Kleine Displays sind gnadenlos. Jede schlampige Designentscheidung springt einem sofort ins Gesicht.~

Die erste Grenze war die Geometrie. Der Verlaufspuffer enthält 24 Werte, daher verwendet das Rendering einen konstanten horizontalen Abstand von drei Pixeln pro Slot.

- ein Wert pro Stunden-Slot
- x-Position mit festem Schritt
- genug Abstand für visuelle Trennung
- trotzdem kompakt genug für 128 Pixel Breite

So bleibt der Graph schmal, berechenbar und lesbar, statt zu einer zusammengestauchten Pixelmasse zu verkommen.

Die zweite Entscheidung betrifft die Reihenfolge der Daten. Intern liegen die Werte in einem 24er-Ringpuffer. Für die Anzeige werden die Daten aber nicht kopiert oder umsortiert. Stattdessen ändert der Renderer nur den Startindex und läuft zyklisch durch das Array.

- Speicherung bleibt simpel
- Darstellung bleibt chronologisch
- kein unnötiges Herumschieben im Speicher
- das sichtbare Fenster rotiert automatisch mit der aktuellen Stunde

Das ist eine dieser kleinen technischen Entscheidungen, die einem später viel Unsinn ersparen.

Für Feuchte und Druck kommt eine **adaptive Skalierung** zum Einsatz. Der Renderer durchsucht die gespeicherten Werte, ignoriert leere Einträge, bestimmt echtes Minimum und Maximum und leitet daraus Mitte und Spannweite ab. Daraus entsteht dann der vertikale Zeichenschritt.

- leere Slots werden übersprungen
- Min und Max stammen aus realen Daten
- die Skala passt sich an die letzten Werte an
- ein Mindestschritt verhindert absurdes Hineinzoomen

Ohne diese Untergrenze würde ein kaum schwankender Druckverlauf dramatischer aussehen als ein Börsencrash. Mit ihr bleibt der Graph ruhig und ehrlich.

Die vertikale Abbildung ist nicht an einer Bodenlinie aufgehängt, sondern um eine Mittellinie organisiert. Werte werden also relativ zu einem Zentrum gezeichnet.

- mittige Skalierung macht Trends besser lesbar
- kleine Schwankungen bleiben sichtbar
- der Graph wirkt ausgewogen statt an einen Rand gequetscht

Gerade bei stabilen Bedingungen ist das entscheidend.

Die Temperatur wird bewusst anders behandelt. Hier gibt es **eine fixe Skala** statt Auto-Zoom.

- visuelle Konsistenz über längere Zeiträume
- leichterer Vergleich zwischen Tagen
- keine irreführende Übertreibung kleiner Änderungen

Ein Temperaturgraph soll nicht hysterisch werden, nur weil sich das Zimmer um ein halbes Grad verändert hat.

Der letzte Baustein ist Kontext. Ein Graph ohne Referenzwerte ist bloß Dekoration, die sich wichtig macht. Deshalb gibt der Renderer rechts drei Leitwerte aus.

- Maximum
- Mittelwert beziehungsweise Mitte, je nach Modus
- Minimum

Die Ausgabe erfolgt im Fixpunktformat. Das hält die Darstellung präzise, ohne überall Float-Formatierung mitzuschleppen.

Beim ersten Start sind manche Verlaufswerte noch leer. Diese Einträge werden schlicht ignoriert.

- keine Müll-Linien
- keine erfundenen Nullwerte
- der Verlauf wächst in den ersten 24 Stunden organisch zusammen

Damit ist die Anzeige schon ab dem ersten Boot robust nutzbar und nicht erst nach einem ganzen Tag.

Am Ende ging es in diesem Teil weniger um hübsche Grafik als um Disziplin. Auf so einem kleinen Display gibt es keinen Platz für visuellen Zierrat. Jede Linie muss Bedeutung tragen.

~Teil VII schließt das Projekt ab: mit Lessons Learned, Tradeoffs und einer ehrlichen Liste jener Dinge, die nach einer V2 verlangen.~
